_meta.purpose: Issue 12 — proves the ORDER BY conditional in eval/compare.py. Row order is canonicalized away (rows sorted on both sides) UNLESS the gold SQL declares it significant via a top-level ORDER BY, in which case a same-rows/wrong-order candidate must be judged incorrect. Detection is sqlglot AST-based, never regex (CLAUDE.md §4).
_meta.format: Same triple format as baseline.json. These cases rely on eval.compare.DEFAULT_RULES (now 'order_insensitive'); none override 'rules'. Scope: ordering only — value-level canonicalization (NULL/float/column/multiset) is Issue 13.
_meta.rule: A canonicalization is applied to BOTH sides identically, so sorting can never make a wrong answer look right (CLAUDE.md domain rule 1).

cases.description: Gold has a top-level ORDER BY; candidate returns the SAME rows in the WRONG order → incorrect. The order error must be caught.
cases.gold_sql: SELECT name FROM merchants ORDER BY signup_date;

cases.description: Gold has a top-level ORDER BY; candidate returns the same rows in the SAME order → correct.
cases.gold_sql: SELECT name FROM merchants ORDER BY signup_date;

cases.description: Gold has NO ORDER BY; candidate returns the same rows in a different order → correct. Row order is not significant, so it is normalized away.
cases.gold_sql: SELECT name FROM merchants WHERE category = 'software';

cases.description: Gold's only ORDER BY is buried in a subquery and does not affect the final row order; candidate reorders the output → correct. Detection must consider only top-level ORDER BY.
cases.gold_sql: SELECT name FROM merchants WHERE id IN (SELECT merchant_id FROM payments ORDER BY amount);

cases.description: Gold has NO ORDER BY; sorting normalizes order but cannot hide a genuinely different multiset of rows → incorrect. Guards that order-insensitivity does not launder wrong answers.
cases.gold_sql: SELECT name FROM merchants WHERE category = 'software';

cases.description: Gold has NO ORDER BY; multi-column rows returned in a different order → correct. Sorting is row-wise across all columns.

Gold's top-level ORDER BY sits on a set operation (UNION); it governs the final output order, so a same-rows/wrong-order candidate → incorrect. Detection must read `order` off the outermost set-op node, not only a bare SELECT.
cases.gold_sql: SELECT name FROM merchants UNION SELECT name FROM partners ORDER BY name;

cases.description: A parenthesized whole query keeps its ORDER BY top-level; after unwrapping the outer Subquery node the order is significant, so a same-rows/wrong-order candidate → incorrect.
cases.gold_sql: (SELECT name FROM merchants ORDER BY signup_date);

cases.description: Gold SQL that sqlglot cannot parse raises ParseError; rather than asserting order matters, detection falls back to order-insensitive, so a different-order candidate → correct. Gold SQL is validated upstream — this is the safe default for a harness bug.
